The Samsung Galaxy Note 7 recall was a 2016 global safety recall after the phone's batteries overheated and caught fire, ending with Samsung permanently discontinuing the phone on October 11, 2016. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission recalled about 1 million U.S. units on September 15, 2016. Samsung estimated the cost at least $5.3 billion through early 2017, per the Associated Press.

 What happened in the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 recall?
 The Samsung Galaxy Note 7 recall was a two-stage recall of a flagship smartphone whose lithium-ion batteries could overheat and catch fire. The phone went on sale in August 2016, and Samsung announced its own recall in early September, according to eWeek.
 The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) made the recall official on September 15, 2016. The CPSC said Samsung had received 92 U.S. reports of batteries overheating, including 26 reports of burns and 55 reports of property damage, among them fires in cars and a garage.
 The replacement phones then had problems of their own. Telecompaper, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported that Samsung told partners to stop all transactions with the new Note 7 in October 2016, then filed with South Korean regulators that it would permanently stop production and sales. Samsung explained the cause in January 2017: two separate battery faults.
 Who was involved in the Note 7 recall?
 The Note 7 recall involved Samsung's mobile leaders, two battery suppliers, independent labs and U.S. regulators. The table lists the main parties and what each did.
 Party Role What each did 
 Samsung Electronics Manufacturer Recalled the phone, discontinued it and published the cause and new safety checks 
 DJ Koh, president of Samsung's mobile communications business Company spokesperson Presented the investigation results in Seoul on January 23, 2017 and apologized to customers and partners 
 Samsung SDI Battery supplier Made the original batteries, whose casing corners were found too small, per PCR 
 Amperex Technology Ltd. (ATL) Battery supplier Made batteries for the replacement phones, which had a welding defect, per MobileSyrup and AP 
 UL, Exponent and TUV Rheinland Independent testing groups Examined the phones and batteries alongside Samsung 
 Elliot Kaye, chairman of the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission Regulator Told reporters on September 15, 2016 that consumers should use the recall right away, per NPR 
 What is the timeline of the Note 7 recall?
 The Note 7 timeline runs from an August 2016 launch to a January 2017 root-cause announcement. The table gives each dated step and its source.
 Date Event Source 
 Aug. 2016 The Galaxy Note 7 goes on sale in the U.S. for $850 to $890 CPSC recall notice 
 Early Sept. 2016 Samsung announces its own recall after about 35 reports of fires worldwide eWeek, Sept. 15, 2016 
 Sept. 15, 2016 The CPSC announces a recall of about 1 million U.S. phones CPSC; NPR, Sept. 15, 2016 
 Sept. 20, 2016 Samsung plans a software update limiting the battery to a 60% charge Engadget, Sept. 15, 2016 
 Oct. 11, 2016 Samsung halts sales and production; about $18 billion in market value is wiped off in one day CNBC, Oct. 12, 2016 
 Oct. 12, 2016 Samsung cuts third-quarter operating profit guidance to 5.2 trillion won from 7.8 trillion won Reuters, via Business Standard 
 Oct. 13, 2016 Samsung forecasts a further hit of about $3 billion over two quarters Reuters, via Fortune 
 Jan. 23, 2017 Samsung announces two separate battery faults and a new 8-Point Battery Safety Check Samsung Newsroom; AP 
 What did Samsung do, and what worked?
 Samsung recalled the phone, stopped sales when replacements also failed, hired outside testers and published the root cause with a new safety process. The last step is the part communicators study.
 The exchange offer was concrete. eWeek reported that Samsung offered a new Note 7 with a different battery, or an exchange for a Galaxy S7 or S7 edge, and the CPSC added a refund option. Engadget reported a software update to limit the battery charge as a stopgap.
 The strongest move came in January 2017. Samsung's press conference named the cause, showed independent reports from UL, Exponent and TUV Rheinland, and described new protocols. Samsung said it implemented multi-layer safety measures and an 8-Point Battery Safety Check and formed a Battery Advisory Group of external experts. The company also said it was taking responsibility for failing to identify the battery design and manufacturing issues.
 The evidence was specific. The AP reported that Samsung and the outside inspectors tested more than 200,000 phones, found defects in two sets of batteries from two manufacturers, and found no evidence that high energy density alone made the phones prone to overheating. PCR reported that the first battery's casing corner was too small, which bent the negative electrode and made short circuits easier, while MobileSyrup reported that the second manufacturer introduced a welding defect while rushing to build replacement batteries.
 The weak point was the first fix. The replacement phones suffered problems, which turned a recall into a discontinuation. Even so, MobileSyrup reported that more than 3 million Note 7 devices had been returned by January 2017, and VentureBeat said more than 96% had been returned.
 What did the Note 7 recall cost?
 The Note 7 recall cost Samsung at least $5.3 billion through early 2017, according to a Samsung estimate reported by the Associated Press. The table lists the sourced figures.
 Item Amount Source 
 Samsung's estimated total cost through early 2017 At least $5.3 billion Associated Press, Jan. 22, 2017 
 Third-quarter operating profit guidance cut From 7.8 trillion won to 5.2 trillion won, about $2.3 billion Reuters, via Business Standard, Oct. 12, 2016 
 Further hit forecast over the next two quarters About $3 billion Reuters, via Fortune, Oct. 13, 2016 
 Market value lost on October 11, 2016 About $18 billion CNBC, Oct. 12, 2016 
 Global phones in the first recall About 2.5 million Engadget, Sept. 15, 2016 
 U.S. phones in the CPSC recall About 1 million CPSC; NPR, Sept. 15, 2016 
 What can brands copy from the Note 7 case?
 Brands can copy four habits from the Note 7 case: investigate with independent testers, name the cause, announce a permanent process change and report return rates. The table links each habit to the evidence.
 Lesson What the case showed What a team can do 
 Use independent testers UL, Exponent and TUV Rheinland examined the phones and batteries Name the labs and publish their reports 
 Name the cause Samsung identified two separate battery faults and explained each Explain the mechanism in plain language, not a general apology 
 Announce a permanent process change Samsung introduced an 8-Point Battery Safety Check and a Battery Advisory Group Describe each new check and who outside the company oversees it 
 Report the return rate Samsung reported more than 96% of Note 7 phones had been returned Publish returns and exchange counts with dates 
 The case also shows the price of a second failure. Because the replacement phones had issues, Samsung moved from a recall to a permanent stop-sale, and the cost estimate grew through October 2016. For Samsung's wider brand story, see the Samsung public relations profile.

 Why did the Galaxy Note 7 catch fire?
 Samsung said two separate battery faults caused the fires. The original batteries had casing corners that were too small, and the replacement batteries had a welding defect, according to PCR and MobileSyrup.
 When was the Note 7 recalled?
 Samsung announced its recall in early September 2016, and the CPSC made it official on September 15, 2016. Samsung permanently discontinued the phone on October 11, 2016.
 How much did the Note 7 recall cost Samsung?
 Samsung estimated the problems would cost at least $5.3 billion through early 2017, according to the Associated Press. Reuters reported a $2.3 billion third-quarter hit and a further forecast of about $3 billion.
 How many Note 7 phones were recalled?
 The CPSC recalled about 1 million phones in the United States, and Engadget reported a global recall of about 2.5 million phones. MobileSyrup reported that more than 3 million devices had been returned by January 2017.
 What did Samsung change after the Note 7?
 Samsung introduced multi-layer safety measures and an 8-Point Battery Safety Check and formed a Battery Advisory Group of outside experts, according to its January 23, 2017 announcement.
